documentation.range: This species occurs throughout northern and central sub-Saharan Africa, from the fringes of the Sahara in Mauritania, Mali and Chad east to Somalia, Eritrea, Ethiopia, western Kenya, Rwanda and Tanzania, with apparently isolated records from central areas of Tanzania (Largen and Spawls 2010, Spawls et al. 2018). The southern limit is in Angola in Central Africa (Largen and Spawls 2010), and northern Tanzania in East Africa (Spawls et al. 2018). It is replaced south of this range, and in central Kenya, eastern Congo, Zambia and Burundi, by the Southern African Python (Python natalensis), although the two species exhibit some overlap in both Tanzania (Spawls et al. 2018) and Angola (Marques et al. 2018) and apparent hybrids from the former area are known (Spawls et al. 2018). It is found in most territories in West Africa.
documentation.population: This species is described as being ubiquitous in forest below the Sahel (Chippaux 2006); however although widespread, it occurs at population densities of approximately 0.2-0.4 individuals per km2 in Nigeria, and 0.1 individuals per km2 in Cameroon, Ghana and Togo (Luiselli et al. 2012). This low density puts it at risk from harvesting pressures as well as habitat loss; in southern regions of Nigeria declines as high as 60% over the past 15 years (likely to be within three generations) have been recorded (G. Akani and L. Luiselli unpubl. data). Significantly, very few individuals of the sizes favoured for harvesting (above 3.5 m) were found following declines. G. Segniagbeto and A. Aidan (unpubl. data) report high, but unquantified, rates of decline in Togo. The snake now appears to be very rare in both countries, and to retain moderate abundance only in inaccessible mangrove forests in Nigeria (L. Luiselli pers. comm. 2012). Due to its association with permanent water, it is rare or absent in arid regions of eastern Ethiopia, eastern Eritrea, and northern and central Somalia (Largen and Spawls 2010). There have been some reductions in local populations in urban centres of Tanzania (K. Howell pers. comm. 2014).
documentation.habitats: This snake is closely-associated with swampy areas and the banks of permanent watercourses (Trape and Mané 2006). In Togo it ranges into the littoral zone, characterized by marshland and mangroves (Segniagbeto et al. 2011). In West Africa it is also known from the moderately dry to arid areas of the Sahelian and Sudan climatic zones (Trape and Mané 2006, Segniagbeto et al. 2011). It is a strong swimmer, and has colonized the offshore Bijágos islands of Guinea-Bissau where it is widespread (Auliya et al. 2012), but will also climb into the trees (Trape and Mané 2006). This nocturnal python is the largest snake in Africa, and preys on mammals and birds, sometimes including livestock (Trape and Mané 2006). In very exceptional cases, the largest animals have been known to prey on human children (Auliya et al. 2012) and, occasionally, adults (Trape and Mané 2006). Generation length is unclear, however this is a large, slow-growing animal, and mark-recapture data indicates that individuals only attain large sizes (4 m and above) at 10–13 years of age (G. Akani and L. Luiselli unpubl. data); conversely Spawls et al. (2018) indicate that this is a fast-growing species and juveniles can reach a length of 1.4 m in a year. This is an oviparous species laying clutches of 60–100 eggs. Captive specimens have lived for more than 27 years (Spawls et al. 2018).
documentation.threats: Exports of this species from Togo have risen rapidly in recent years, but it is not known whether harvesting for the pet trade has yet reached or is likely to reach a level that is unsustainable in this country, or whether this reflects trends throughout the snake's very wide range. Most of the pet trade specimens appear to be hatchlings. This species is, however, very popular as bushmeat (e.g. Fuashi et al. 2019, Eniang et al. 2008, Jensen et al. 2017), and, at national and local scales, for use in leather manufacture (L. Luiselli pers. comm. 2012). There is, however, no skin trade from East Africa (K. Howell pers. comm. 2014). Most trade occurs at national and sub-national level, for which no figures are available, and as such the relatively small numbers of animals reported in international trade (e.g. from Tanzania - UNEP 2007) are not representative of actual levels of exploitation. This is a slow-growing species which occurs in low population densities, and harvesting for skins and meat preferentially targets animals 4 m and above in length (corresponding to an age of 10–13 years - G. Akani and L. Luiselli unpubl. data), and this preferential harvesting of larger animals is likely to have negative effects on the viability of subpopulations of this snake. The species is also heavily used in traditional medicine in Cameroon and much of West Africa. A further major threat exists from deforestation, as this species is often found in primary, secondary and gallery forest habitats (L. Luiselli pers. comm. 2012, Luiselli et al. 2012). Due to its wide range and presence in a number of large protected areas, it is not thought to be at risk in East Africa despite pressures from development (Spawls et al. 2018). This species is subject to some degree of persecution, as it is perceived as a threat to livestock and potentially to humans, however, in some areas traditional beliefs discourage killing these snakes (Spawls et al. 2018).
documentation.measures: This species is listed on CITES Appendix II. Further research into the impacts of harvesting of this species is recommended for West and Central Africa. It occurs in a number of protected areas.
documentation.use_trade: This python is heavily exploited commercially for leather and food, as its meat is prized by local people within its range (Luiselli and Akani 2002, Chippaux 2006). Between 2006 and 2018, more than 209,000 P. sebae-derived products were exported. It is used intensively in traditional medicine in Cameroon, Nigeria, Benin, Togo and Ghana (L. Luiselli pers. comm. 2012, Segniagbeto et al. 2013). It is not actively hunted for food or skins in East Africa.
documentation.rationale: This species is heavily-exploited throughout its West African range, particularly for bushmeat and leather, and high rates of decline have been reported within West Africa.  Where quantifiable, in West Africa these declines appear to exceed 60% over three generations (a generation estimated as likely to be in excess of 15 years for this long-lived snake). There are unlikely to be substantial declines in East Africa, and it is uncertain whether global declines of between 30–50% over three generations are likely. Further research is needed to quantify declines in this species, and it is tentatively listed as Near Threatened here pending these studies.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: The southern African taxon Python sebae natalensis was elevated to full species status by Broadley (1999). A phylogenetic analysis (K. A. Tolley, Unpublished data 2019) supports the treatment of P. natalensis and P. sebae as full species.
